prompt: By the section's definition, what happens to carbon in an organic oxidation?

choices.text: It loses electron density, by forming a bond to O, N or a halogen or by breaking a bond to H
It gains electron density, by forming a bond to H or by breaking a bond to O, N or a halogen
choices.why: That describes an organic reduction.

choices.text: It loses electron density, by forming a bond to H or by breaking a bond to O, N or a halogen
choices.why: Forming a bond to H, which is less electronegative, adds electron density to carbon; breaking a bond to O, N or X does too.

choices.text: It gains electron density, by forming a bond to O, N or a halogen or by breaking a bond to H
choices.why: These changes do happen in an oxidation, but they decrease the electron density on carbon.

explanation: An organic oxidation results in a loss of electron density by carbon, caused either by bond formation between carbon and a more electronegative atom (usually O, N or a halogen) or by bond-breaking between carbon and a less electronegative atom (usually H).

prompt: Which change makes a reaction an organic reduction?

choices.text: Forming a C–H bond, or breaking a C–O, C–N or C–X bond
Forming a C–O, C–N or C–X bond
choices.why: Forming a bond to a more electronegative atom decreases electron density on carbon: that is an oxidation.

choices.text: Breaking a C–H bond
choices.why: Breaking a bond to the less electronegative H decreases electron density on carbon: that is an oxidation.

choices.text: Forming one C–H bond and one C–X bond at the same time
choices.why: These changes cancel. Adding HBr to an alkene this way is neither an oxidation nor a reduction.

explanation: An organic reduction results in a gain of electron density by carbon, caused either by bond formation between carbon and a less electronegative atom (forming C–H) or by bond-breaking between carbon and a more electronegative atom (breaking C–O, C–N or C–X).

prompt: Is the radical chlorination of methane to give chloromethane an oxidation, a reduction or neither?

choices.text: An oxidation, because a C–H bond is broken and a C–Cl bond is formed
A reduction, because the C–H bond of methane is broken
choices.why: Breaking a bond between carbon and the less electronegative H decreases electron density on carbon: an oxidation.

choices.text: Neither, because one atom is simply substituted for another
choices.why: A substitution can change the oxidation level. Here H is replaced by the more electronegative Cl.

choices.text: A reduction, because HCl is formed as a by-product of the reaction
choices.why: What counts is the change at carbon: it loses a C–H bond and gains a C–Cl bond.

explanation: The chlorination of methane to yield chloromethane is an oxidation because a C–H bond is broken and a C–Cl bond is formed. Both changes decrease electron density on carbon.

prompt: Chloromethane is converted into methane by forming the Grignard reagent and then protonating it. Is this overall change an oxidation, a reduction or neither?

choices.text: A reduction, because a C–Cl bond is broken and a C–H bond is formed
An oxidation, because the C–Cl bond of chloromethane is broken
choices.why: Breaking a bond to a more electronegative atom increases electron density on carbon: a reduction.

choices.text: Neither, because chlorine is simply swapped for hydrogen
choices.why: Swapping Cl for H changes the bonds at carbon in the reduction direction: one C–Cl bond lost, one C–H bond gained.

choices.text: An oxidation, because magnesium metal is used in the first step
choices.why: What counts is the change at carbon. Overall, a C–Cl bond becomes a C–H bond, which is a reduction.

explanation: The conversion of an alkyl chloride to an alkane via a Grignard reagent followed by protonation is a reduction, because a C–Cl bond is broken and a C–H bond is formed.

prompt: Is the reaction of ethylene with Br2 to give 1,2-dibromoethane an oxidation, a reduction or neither?

choices.text: An oxidation, because two C–Br bonds are formed
Neither, because addition reactions never change the oxidation level
choices.why: Some additions don't (HBr adds one C–H and one C–Br bond), but Br2 adds two C–Br bonds and no C–H bond.

choices.text: A reduction, because the C=C π bond is broken
choices.why: Carbon–carbon bonds don't count in the definitions. Forming two C–Br bonds is an oxidation.

choices.text: A reduction, because bromine atoms are added to carbon
choices.why: Forming bonds to a more electronegative atom such as Br decreases electron density on carbon: an oxidation.

explanation: The reaction of an alkene with Br2 to yield a 1,2-dibromide is an oxidation because two C–Br bonds are formed.

prompt: Is the reaction of ethylene with HBr to give bromoethane an oxidation, a reduction or neither?

choices.text: Neither, because one C–H bond and one C–Br bond are formed
An oxidation, because the more electronegative Br bonds to carbon
choices.why: A C–H bond forms at the same time and offsets it, so the level doesn't change.

choices.text: A reduction, because a hydrogen atom bonds to carbon
choices.why: A C–Br bond forms at the same time and offsets it, so the level doesn't change.

choices.text: An oxidation, because the double bond is broken
choices.why: Breaking the C=C bond doesn't count. One C–H and one C–Br bond form, so the change is neither.

explanation: The reaction of an alkene with HBr to yield an alkyl bromide is neither an oxidation nor a reduction because both a C–H and a C–Br bond are formed.

prompt: Why are alkanes at the lowest oxidation level and CO2 at the highest?

choices.text: Alkanes have the most C–H bonds per carbon; CO2 has the most C–O bonds
Alkanes are the least polar compounds, and CO2 is the most polar
choices.why: Polarity isn't the measure (CO2 has no net dipole moment at all). What matters is C–H versus C–O bonds per carbon.

choices.text: Alkanes are the most reactive compounds, and CO2 is the least reactive
choices.why: Oxidation level is set by the kinds of bonds to carbon, not by reactivity.

choices.text: Alkanes have the most C–C bonds per carbon, and CO2 has no C–C bonds
choices.why: C–C bonds don't count. Alkanes have the maximum number of C–H bonds per carbon, CO2 the maximum number of C–O bonds.

explanation: Alkanes are at the lowest oxidation level because they have the maximum possible number of C–H bonds per carbon, and CO2 is at the highest level because it has the maximum possible number of C–O bonds per carbon (Figure 10.8.1).

prompt: Compounds with the same number of carbons can be compared by adding their C–O, C–N and C–X bonds and subtracting their C–H bonds, as in Worked Example 10.8.1. What value does this give for propane, CH3CH2CH3?
explanation: Propane has no C–O, C–N or C–X bonds and eight C–H bonds: 0 − 8 = −8. That is the lowest of the four compounds in Worked Example 10.8.1, as expected for an alkane.

prompt: Compounds with the same number of carbons can be compared by adding their C–O, C–N and C–X bonds and subtracting their C–H bonds, as in Worked Example 10.8.1. What value does this give for 2-propanol, (CH3)2CHOH?
explanation: 2-Propanol has one C–O bond and seven C–H bonds: 1 − 7 = −6. Propene, with six C–H bonds, also gets −6, so the two are at the same oxidation level (Worked Example 10.8.1).

prompt: Compounds with the same number of carbons can be compared by adding their C–O, C–N and C–X bonds and subtracting their C–H bonds, as in Worked Example 10.8.1, counting the C=O double bond as two C–O bonds. What value does this give for acetone, (CH3)2C=O?
explanation: Acetone has two C–O bonds (its C=O) and six C–H bonds: 2 − 6 = −4. That puts it above propene and 2-propanol (−6) and propane (−8), making it the highest of the four in Worked Example 10.8.1.

prompt: Compounds with the same number of carbons can be compared by adding their C–O, C–N and C–X bonds and subtracting their C–H bonds, as in Worked Example 10.8.1, counting a C≡N triple bond as three C–N bonds. What value does this give for acetonitrile, CH3C≡N?
explanation: Acetonitrile has three C–N bonds (its C≡N) and three C–H bonds: 3 − 3 = 0. That is higher than ethylenediamine, H2NCH2CH2NH2 (2 − 4 = −2), and ethylamine, CH3CH2NH2 (1 − 5 = −4), matching the order in Exercise 10.8.1b.

prompt: Using the method of Worked Example 10.8.1, which of these six-carbon compounds has the highest oxidation level?

choices.text: Benzene, C6H6
Cyclohexanone, C6H10O, which has one C=O
choices.why: Two C–O bonds (its C=O) minus ten C–H bonds gives −8, lower than benzene's −6.

choices.text: 1-Chlorocyclohexene, C6H9Cl
choices.why: One C–Cl bond minus nine C–H bonds gives −8, lower than benzene's −6.

choices.text: Cyclohexane, C6H12
choices.why: Twelve C–H bonds and nothing else gives −12, the lowest of the four.

explanation: Benzene has only six C–H bonds and nothing to subtract them from: −6. Cyclohexanone (2 − 10 = −8) and 1-chlorocyclohexene (1 − 9 = −8) tie below it, and cyclohexane (−12) is lowest, as in Exercise 10.8.1a.

prompt: Is the conversion of 2-methyl-2-propanol, (CH3)3COH, into 2-chloro-2-methylpropane, (CH3)3CCl, with HCl an oxidation, a reduction or neither?

choices.text: Neither, because a C–O bond is broken and a C–Cl bond is formed
An oxidation, because a new bond from carbon to chlorine is formed
choices.why: A C–O bond is broken at the same time, so the oxidation level stays the same (1 − 9 = −8 for both).

choices.text: A reduction, because the bond from carbon to oxygen is broken
choices.why: A C–Cl bond forms at the same time, so the oxidation level doesn't change.

choices.text: A reduction, because water is formed as a by-product of the reaction
choices.why: What counts is carbon's bonds: one bond to an electronegative atom (O) is traded for another (Cl).

explanation: Carbon loses a C–O bond (a reduction-type change) but gains a C–Cl bond (an oxidation-type change). Both compounds have one bond to an electronegative atom and nine C–H bonds, so both are at level −8 and the reaction is neither an oxidation nor a reduction.

prompt: Propanal, CH3CH2CHO, is converted into 1-propanol, CH3CH2CH2OH, by NaBH4 in water. Is this an oxidation, a reduction or neither?

choices.text: A reduction, because a C–H bond forms and a C–O bond is lost
An oxidation, because a new O–H bond forms in the product
choices.why: O–H bonds don't involve carbon. Carbon gains a C–H bond and loses one C–O bond, so the level falls from −4 to −6.

choices.text: Neither, because H2 is simply added across a double bond
choices.why: Adding hydrogen to C=O trades a C–O bond for a C–H bond, so the level drops from −4 to −6.

choices.text: An oxidation, because the product still contains an oxygen atom
choices.why: Both compounds contain one oxygen. What matters is that a C–H bond forms and a C–O bond is broken.

explanation: Propanal has two C–O bonds (its C=O) and six C–H bonds (2 − 6 = −4); 1-propanol has one C–O bond and seven C–H bonds (1 − 7 = −6). The level goes down, so the reaction is a reduction (Exercise 10.8.2a).

prompt: Cyclohexene is converted into cyclohexanol by reaction with BH3 followed by NaOH and H2O2. Is this an oxidation, a reduction or neither?

choices.text: Neither, because one C–H bond and one C–O bond are formed
An oxidation, because a C–O bond forms and H2O2 is used
choices.why: A C–H bond forms at the same time, so the oxidation level stays at −10.

choices.text: A reduction, because a new C–H bond is formed at carbon
choices.why: A C–O bond forms at the same time, so the oxidation level doesn't change.

choices.text: A reduction, because the carbon–carbon double bond is lost
choices.why: C–C bonds don't count. One C–H and one C–O bond form, so the change is neither.

explanation: Cyclohexene, C6H10, has ten C–H bonds (−10). Cyclohexanol has one C–O bond and eleven C–H bonds (1 − 11 = −10). The level doesn't change, so the reaction is neither an oxidation nor a reduction (Exercise 10.8.2b).
